raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old man with no relevant past medical history presented to the eye casualty service complaining of sudden onset central 'white ring' and decreased vision in the right eye (RE) over the past seven days. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/12 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye (LE). Intraocular pressure was 14 mmHg in both eyes. Examination of the RE showed no cells in the right anterior chamber and 1+ vitreous cells; fundus examination revealed a yellow placoid lesion involving the macular area with no signs of vasculitis or retinal necrosis. Examination of the LE was unremarkable.
MMI of the retina including colour fundus photograph, fundus autofluorescence, SD-OCT, fluorescein angiography and indocyanine green angiography are presented in Figure 1 (Fig. 1), Figure 2 (Fig. 2), and Figure 3 (Fig. 3).
The medical history was carefully reviewed; the patient admitted to be addicted to poppers and cocaine, and reported promiscuous homosexual activity over the last months. He denied intravenous drug use and any systemic symptoms such as headache, skin rash, nausea, weight loss, cough, or night sweats. A complete laboratory work-up was ordered, including TB QuantiFERON-TB testing, syphilis serology and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibodies. Seven days after presentation, the patient reported spontaneous improvement in the vision of the RE, and BCVA improved to 6/9 in the RE and was stable in the LE. Full blood count, liver function test, kidney function, angiotensin-converting enzyme level were within normal range, HIV antibodies were negative. However, results for QuantiFERON-TB testing and syphilis had not been available yet. MMI revealed spontaneous improvement of the placoid lesion (Figure 2 (Fig. 2), Figure 3 (Fig. 3)).
Two weeks after presentation, BCVA further improved to 6/6 in the RE and MMI showed signs of early resolution of the placoid lesion. Laboratory results returned negative for QuantiFERON-TB testing, and positive for venereal disease research laboratory test and fluorescent treponemal antibody testing. Therefore, a definite diagnosis of ASPPC was made, and the patient was promptly referred to the Infectious Disease Department for systemic treatment with penicillin.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old man presented with a 7-day history of a sudden-onset central 'white ring' scotoma and decreased vision in his right eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Seven days prior to presentation, the patient noticed an acute central white ring and blurred vision in his right eye (BCVA 6/12). Over the subsequent 2 weeks, while awaiting infectious serology results without any antibiotic or steroid therapy, his right-eye vision spontaneously improved to 6/9 at day 7 and 6/6 at day 14 alongside spontaneous regression of the macular placoid lesion.
subjective.past_medical_history: No relevant medical history. Detailed social history revealed addiction to inhaled alkyl nitrites ('poppers') and intranasal cocaine, as well as promiscuous unprotected homosexual activity over the preceding months; denied intravenous drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right central visual disturbance; negative for headache, skin rash, nausea, weight loss, cough, or night sweats.

objective.physical_examination: Initial best-corrected visual acuity was 6/12 in the right eye (RE, spontaneously improving to 6/9 at 1 week and 6/6 at 2 weeks) and 6/6 in the left eye (LE), with intraocular pressures of 14 mmHg OU. Right-eye examination showed a quiet anterior chamber, 1+ vitreous cells, and a large yellowish outer-retinal placoid lesion involving the macula without retinal necrosis or vasculitis; the left eye was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, liver and kidney function tests, serum ACE level, HIV antibodies, and QuantiFERON-TB testing were all normal or negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Multimodal retinal imaging (color fundus photography, fundus autofluorescence [FAF], SD-OCT, fluorescein angiography [FA], and indocyanine green angiography [ICGA]) demonstrated characteristic outer retinal/ellipsoid zone disruption, hyperautofluorescence, and choriocapillaris hypofluorescence across the right macular placoid lesion, followed by spontaneous anatomical recovery over 14 days.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed right acute syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinitis (ASPPC) exhibiting spontaneous clinical and multimodal-imaging resolution prior to antibiotic initiation, established via positive serum VDRL and positive FTA-ABS tests (tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and HIV excluded). Promptly referred to the infectious diseases department for systemic parenteral penicillin therapy.
